lessons.title: Secure architecture principles and defense in depth
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a fortified castle with several walls: a moat, a first wall, a second wall and a keep in the center holding a safe.
objectives: Explain defense in depth and its three families of controls.
Apply the main secure design principles (least privilege, secure by default, fail secure…).
Reduce the attack surface of a system.
Recognize a design that relies on a single point of failure.

references.title: Saltzer and Schroeder, "The Protection of Information in Computer Systems", 1975 (design principles)
NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 1, Engineering Trustworthy Secure Systems

blocks.text: Thinking about security from the design stage

A secure architecture is not a list of products: it is a way of organizing components so that one mistake, one flaw or one attacker is not enough to compromise everything. Building security in from the design stage (security by design) costs much less than adding it after going into production.

blocks.title: Defense in depth (défense en profondeur)
blocks.text: Stacking of independent controls of different kinds, so that a failure of one is compensated by the others. It is also called layered security.

blocks.title: The layers of defense, from the outside to the data
blocks.alt: Six-step diagram going from the outside to the center: policies and awareness, physical security, network perimeter, internal network, host, application, and finally the data at the center.

rows: Policies, awareness, separation of duties, background checks

blocks.text: Defense in depth = fortified castle: moat, ramparts, second wall, keep. The attacker must get through every layer; one is enough to stop them.
The main design principles

rows: Just the rights needed, just for the time needed
A web service without administrator rights
The shipped configuration is the safest one
On failure, the system denies access rather than opening it
Keep it simple: what is simple can be verified
Every access is checked, every time
No right kept in cache indefinitely
Security does not rely on the secrecy of the design
Several conditions for a critical action

blocks.title: Fail secure or fail safe?
blocks.text: For information, fail secure (fail closed) is preferred: on failure, block. But human life always comes first: an emergency exit door must open in case of fire (fail safe). In the exam, people's safety always wins.

blocks.title: The single point of failure
blocks.text: A single firewall, a single administrator who knows everything, a single Internet link: if that element fails or is compromised, everything fails. Redundancy and diversity (two manufacturers, two trained people) reduce this risk.

blocks.title: Reducing the attack surface
items: Disable unneeded services, ports and accounts.
Apply hardening guides (for example the CIS Benchmarks) and track deviations.
Limit administration interfaces to a dedicated network.
Remove obsolete software and versions.

blocks.text: Architecture questions often ask for "the best principle". Spot the keyword: "just the rights needed" → least privilege; "several layers" → defense in depth; "on failure" → fail secure or fail safe; "does not depend on the secrecy of the algorithm" → open design.

blocks.title: SOC case: only one layer gave way
blocks.text: An employee clicks on a malicious attachment: awareness failed. But the workstation has no administrator rights (least privilege), the EDR blocks the execution of a credential-stealing tool, and segmentation prevents the workstation from reaching the payroll servers. The incident stays limited to one workstation, reinstalled in an hour: defense in depth worked.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: Architect: every new application goes through a security design review.
SOC analyst: several layers give several chances to detect the attacker.
Auditor: I look for single points of failure and overly powerful accounts.
CISO: defense in depth is justified by risk, not by piling up products.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Security through obscurity is not a sufficient control (open design).
Fail secure = block on failure; but people's safety comes first.
Defense in depth = different and independent controls, not three identical firewalls.
Least privilege also applies to service accounts and applications.
Defense in depth: administrative, technical and physical layers.
Principles: least privilege, secure by default, fail secure, simplicity, complete mediation, open design.
Reduce the attack surface and avoid single points of failure.
Human life comes before the protection of information.

lessons.title: Security models and trusted components
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a three-story building marked secret, confidential and public, with a crossed-out arrow going up (no read up) and a crossed-out arrow going down (no write down).
objectives: Explain the trusted computing base and the reference monitor.
Apply the rules of Bell-LaPadula (confidentiality) and Biba (integrity).
Recognize the Clark-Wilson and Brewer-Nash models.
Place the trusted hardware components: protection rings, TPM, secure boot.

blocks.text: What we trust

blocks.title: TCB, trusted computing base (base informatique de confiance)
blocks.text: All the hardware, software and firmware on which the security of a system depends. If an element of the TCB is compromised, the security policy can no longer be guaranteed. The aim is therefore to keep it small.

blocks.title: Reference monitor (moniteur de référence)
blocks.text: Abstract concept that controls every access by a subject (user, process) to an object (file, resource). It must be tamperproof, always invoked and small enough to be verified. The security kernel is its implementation.
Reference monitor: "always called, never tampered with, easy to verify".
The formal models

rows: No read up (simple security), no write down (star property *)
No read down, no write up
Access to data only through well-formed transactions; separation of duties; audit log
After viewing a client's data, you no longer access their competitor's

blocks.title: Bell-LaPadula and Biba: two mirrors
blocks.alt: Four-cell table: Bell-LaPadula forbids reading up and writing down to protect confidentiality; Biba forbids reading down and writing up to protect integrity.

blocks.title: Remembering the direction of the arrows
blocks.text: Bell-LaPadula protects secrets: you do not read above your level, and you do not write below it so that information does not leak. Biba protects the purity of data: you do not read a less reliable source, and you do not write into data more reliable than yourself. Biba is the exact opposite of Bell-LaPadula.
BLP = secrets: "I don't read above, I don't gossip below". Biba = integrity: "I don't drink the dirty water from below, I don't pollute the spring above".
Trusted hardware components

rows: Processor privilege levels: ring 0 for the kernel, ring 3 for applications
Chip that stores keys, measures boot and protects disk encryption
Only signed boot loaders and kernels can run
Dedicated device that generates and protects cryptographic keys
A process does not read another one's memory

blocks.text: For virtualization, remember VM escape: a hypervisor flaw lets an attacker break out of a VM to reach the host or the other VMs. The hypervisor is therefore part of the TCB: priority patches and isolated administration.

blocks.title: SOC case: a consulting firm and its competing clients
blocks.text: In a simulated consulting firm, a consultant working for bank A tries to open the file of bank B, its direct competitor. Document management applies a Brewer-Nash type rule: access is denied and an alert is created. The analyst checks that it is a handling error, and the compliance officer confirms that the rule did its job.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: Architect: I keep the TCB as small as possible so that it can be verified.
SOC analyst: an alert on boot integrity (TPM, Secure Boot) always has priority.
Auditor: I check that accounting data is modified only through controlled transactions (Clark-Wilson).
CISO: formal models guide the choice of access controls for sensitive systems.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Bell-LaPadula = confidentiality; Biba = integrity; do not mix them up.
Star property (*) of BLP = no write down.
Clark-Wilson = well-formed transactions and separation of duties.
Brewer-Nash = Chinese wall, conflicts of interest.
TCB: everything security depends on; reference monitor: always invoked, tamperproof, verifiable.
BLP (confidentiality): no read up, no write down. Biba (integrity): no read down, no write up.
Clark-Wilson: well-formed transactions; Brewer-Nash: conflicts of interest.
Rings, TPM, Secure Boot, HSM: trust starts in the hardware.

lessons.title: Zero Trust and modern architectures
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a checkpoint gate in front of each door of a corridor: a person shows a badge and a laptop at each door, even inside the building.
objectives: Explain why the perimeter model is no longer enough.
Describe the principles and components of Zero Trust (decision point, enforcement point).
Name the pillars of a Zero Trust approach.
Apply the cloud shared responsibility model.

references.title: CISA, Zero Trust Maturity Model, version 2.0 (2023)

blocks.text: The end of the castle?

The perimeter model trusts everything that is "inside". Yet users work remotely, applications are in the cloud, and an attacker who has stolen credentials is already inside. Zero Trust starts from the opposite idea: no implicit trust based on network location.

blocks.title: Zero Trust
blocks.text: Security approach in which no user, device or flow is considered trustworthy by default, even inside the network. Every access to a resource is explicitly verified, at each session, based on identity, device state and context.
Zero Trust: "Never trust, always verify" and "assume breach".

rows: Strong identity (MFA), device state, location, time, behavior
Access limited to one resource, for one session, just what is needed
Microsegment, encrypt, monitor continuously, limit movement
You access an application, not the whole network

blocks.text: The components (NIST SP 800-207)

blocks.title: Every request goes through a decision
blocks.alt: Four-step diagram: a subject (user and device) requests access, the policy enforcement point intercepts, the decision point evaluates identity, device and context, then access to the resource is granted for this session only.

blocks.title: PDP and PEP
blocks.text: The policy decision point (PDP), made up of the policy engine and the policy administrator, decides whether to grant access. The policy enforcement point (PEP) sits in front of the resource and opens or closes the connection according to that decision.
The pillars of a Zero Trust approach

The CISA maturity model organizes the approach into five pillars: identity, devices, networks, applications and workloads, data. Three capabilities cut across all of them: visibility and analytics, automation and orchestration, governance. You progress pillar by pillar; Zero Trust is a journey, not a product.

blocks.title: Zero Trust cannot be bought
blocks.text: No single product "does" Zero Trust. It is a strategy that combines identity management, MFA, device management, microsegmentation, encryption and continuous monitoring. Beware of an exam answer that presents a single tool as the solution.
Modern architectures: cloud and access

rows: Operating system, patches, applications, data, identities
The same + operating system and runtime platform
Almost everything, up to the application
Data, accounts, access rights, sharing configuration

blocks.title: Shared responsibility (responsabilité partagée)
blocks.text: Whatever the model, the customer remains responsible for its data and for access management. A leak caused by cloud storage opened to the public by mistake is the customer's fault, not the provider's.

ZTNA (Zero Trust network access) often replaces the VPN: the user only reaches authorized applications, never the whole network. SASE brings together network and security functions in a cloud service (ZTNA, web gateway, CASB, firewall as a service).
Make the link with the previous chapter: microsegmentation is the network translation of Zero Trust, and ZTNA is the evolution of VPN remote access. Questions readily mix the two chapters.

blocks.title: SOC case: stolen credentials are no longer enough
blocks.text: In a simulated exercise, an attacker uses an accountant's stolen password. The decision point notices an unknown, unmanaged device and a connection from an unusual country: it requires MFA, which the attacker cannot provide, and denies access to the payroll application. The SOC receives the alert, forces a password reset and checks that no other resource was reached.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: I present Zero Trust as a multi-year roadmap, pillar by pillar.
Architect: I start with identity and the device inventory, without which no decision is reliable.
SOC analyst: every PDP decision is a valuable log for detecting anomalies.
Auditor: in the cloud, I first check what remains the customer's responsibility: data, access, configuration.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Zero Trust ≠ "no trust in users": it means "no implicit trust".
PDP decides, PEP enforces.
In every cloud model, data and access remain the customer's responsibility.
Being inside the network gives no rights in Zero Trust.
Zero Trust: verify explicitly, least privilege, assume breach, per-resource access.
NIST SP 800-207: PDP (policy engine and administrator) and PEP.
CISA: identity, devices, networks, applications and workloads, data.
Cloud: shared responsibility; ZTNA and SASE modernize access.

flashcards.back: Independent layered controls: administrative, technical, physical.
Just the rights needed, for just the time needed.
The delivered configuration is the most secure one.
Block on failure / open to protect people. People first.
Security does not rely on the secrecy of the design.
Every access is checked, every time.
Everything that is exposed; reducing it = removing what is unneeded.
An element whose failure brings everything down. Countermeasure: redundancy.
Everything security depends on; keep it small.
Always invoked, tamperproof, verifiable.
Confidentiality: no read up, no write down.
Integrity: no read down, no write up.
Well-formed transactions, separation of duties, auditing.
Chinese Wall: conflicts of interest.
Chip: keys, boot measurement, disk encryption.
Never trust, always verify; assume breach.
Policy decision point / policy enforcement point.
Identity, devices, networks, applications and workloads, data.
IaaS, PaaS, SaaS: data and access always belong to the customer.
Per-application access / networking and security delivered as a cloud service.

revisionSheet: # Revision sheet: secure architecture, defense in depth and Zero Trust
Defense in depth: independent, different, layered controls; administrative, technical and physical families.
Principles: least privilege, secure by default, fail secure, economy of mechanism, complete mediation, open design, separation of privilege, reduced attack surface.
Fail secure (block on failure) for information; fail safe (open) when lives are at stake: people first.
Avoid single points of failure: redundancy, vendor diversity, several trained people.
TCB: the hardware, software and firmware that security depends on; keep it small.
Reference monitor: always invoked, tamperproof, verifiable; implemented by the security kernel.
Bell-LaPadula (confidentiality): no read up, no write down (* property).
Biba (integrity): no read down, no write up.
Clark-Wilson: well-formed transactions, separation of duties, auditing. Brewer-Nash: Chinese Wall, conflicts of interest.
Trusted hardware: protection rings (0 kernel, 3 applications), TPM, Secure Boot, HSM. VM escape: the hypervisor is part of the TCB.
Zero Trust: no implicit trust based on the network; verify explicitly, least privilege per session, assume breach.
NIST SP 800-207: the PDP (policy engine and policy administrator) decides, the PEP enforces.
CISA: pillars identity, devices, networks, applications and workloads, data; cross-cutting: visibility, automation, governance.
Cloud: shared responsibility; in IaaS, PaaS or SaaS, the customer remains responsible for its data and access.
ZTNA: per-application access (the evolution of VPN). SASE: networking and security functions delivered as a cloud service.
Pairs not to confuse: BLP/Biba; PDP/PEP; fail secure/fail safe; IaaS/PaaS/SaaS; VPN/ZTNA.

questions.prompt: What is defense in depth?
choices: A single, very powerful firewall placed at the network entrance
Storing backups in a protected underground room
Systematic encryption of every disk in the fleet
Independent, layered controls that compensate for one another
questions.explanation: Several layers of different kinds: if one gives way, the others stop or detect the attacker.

whyNot.0: A single control is a single point of failure.
whyNot.1: A play on words with no connection.
whyNot.2: Encryption is only one layer among others.

questions.prompt: A service account only needs to read one table. Which principle requires giving it only that right?
questions.explanation: Least privilege gives just the rights needed, for just the time needed.

whyNot.1: Economy of mechanism asks you to keep things simple.
whyNot.2: Open design concerns the secrecy of the design.
whyNot.3: Fail safe concerns behavior in the event of a failure.

questions.prompt: Employee awareness training is a control from which family?
questions.explanation: Policies, awareness training and procedures are administrative controls.

whyNot.0: Physical controls protect premises and equipment.
whyNot.1: Technical controls are implemented through technology.
whyNot.2: That is not a control family in this classification.

questions.prompt: In the event of a fire, the badge-controlled doors of a room open automatically. Which principle applies?
choices: Fail safe, because the safety of people comes first
Least privilege, because only authorized badges are accepted
Complete mediation, because every passage is checked
Fail secure, because the information in the room is protected first
questions.explanation: Human life always comes first: exits must open in an emergency.

whyNot.2: Complete mediation concerns checking every access.
whyNot.3: Fail secure would keep the doors locked: unacceptable for people.

questions.prompt: A vendor claims its product is secure "because nobody knows its algorithm". Which principle is violated?
choices: Least privilege: everyone should have only the rights they need
Separation of privilege: a sensitive action requires several conditions
Open design: security must not rely on the secrecy of the design
Secure by default: the delivered configuration must be the most secure one
questions.explanation: Security through obscurity does not hold up: only the key should remain secret (Kerckhoffs).

whyNot.0: Least privilege concerns rights.
whyNot.1: Separation of privilege requires several conditions.
whyNot.3: Secure by default concerns the delivered configuration.

questions.prompt: A firewall fails. To protect the information, which behavior is preferable?
questions.explanation: Fail secure blocks access rather than opening it in the event of a failure.

whyNot.0: That is fail open: the protection disappears.
whyNot.1: A test mode is not a secure failure behavior.
whyNot.2: Logs are valuable during an incident.

questions.prompt: Which action most directly reduces the attack surface of a server?
choices: Adding a logon screen with a legal warning
Uninstalling unneeded services and closing unneeded ports
Renaming the server to make it less visible
Adding RAM to better withstand attacks
questions.explanation: Fewer exposed services, fewer possible flaws.

whyNot.0: No effect on security.
whyNot.2: That is obscurity, not a real reduction.

questions.prompt: A single administrator knows the passwords of all the network devices. Which risks follow? (several answers)
choices: A single point of failure if this person is absent
No separation of duties or mutual oversight
Higher risk if this person acts maliciously
questions.explanation: A single person who is both indispensable and all-powerful combines availability, fraud and knowledge-loss risks.

whyNot.0: Traceability is not improved; it depends on the logs, not on the number of people.

questions.prompt: Which option best illustrates true defense in depth?
choices: A policy of long passwords, changed every month
An up-to-date antivirus installed on every workstation
Three identical firewalls from the same vendor, placed in series
MFA, network segmentation, EDR on the workstations and offline backups
questions.explanation: Different controls, at different layers, that do not share the same weaknesses.

whyNot.0: A single administrative layer.
whyNot.1: A single layer, even if repeated.
whyNot.2: Three identical products share the same flaw.

questions.prompt: A new device is delivered with all services enabled and a well-known administrator password. Which principle is not followed?
questions.explanation: The delivered configuration should be the most secure one: services closed, a unique password to change.

whyNot.0: Open design concerns the secrecy of the design.
whyNot.1: Complete mediation concerns checking every access.

questions.prompt: What does the trusted computing base (TCB) refer to?
choices: The list of users considered trustworthy
The internal network protected by the perimeter firewall
The service contract signed with the cloud provider
The hardware and software components on which security depends
questions.explanation: If an element of the TCB is compromised, the security policy is no longer guaranteed.

whyNot.0: The TCB is technical, not a list of people.
whyNot.1: The internal network is not trusted in itself.
whyNot.2: A contract is not a technical component.

questions.prompt: Under Bell-LaPadula, can a user cleared for "confidential" read a "secret" document?
choices: Yes, but they cannot print it
Yes, if they are in a hurry
questions.explanation: The Bell-LaPadula simple security rule forbids reading above your clearance level.

whyNot.0: Reading itself is forbidden.
whyNot.1: Urgency does not change the rule.
whyNot.2: The rule comes from Bell-LaPadula, which protects confidentiality.

questions.prompt: Which model forbids writing to data with a higher integrity level?
questions.explanation: Biba protects integrity: no read down, no write up.

whyNot.2: Brewer-Nash deals with conflicts of interest.

questions.prompt: What does the Bell-LaPadula star (*) property mean?
questions.explanation: Forbidding writing down prevents copying a secret into a less protected document.

whyNot.0: That is the simple security rule.
whyNot.2: That is a Biba rule.
whyNot.3: MFA is not part of the model.

questions.prompt: Which model requires that accounting data only be modified by well-formed transactions, with separation of duties?
questions.explanation: Clark-Wilson protects commercial integrity through controlled transformation programs and separation of duties.

whyNot.0: Brewer-Nash concerns conflicts of interest.
whyNot.3: Take-Grant describes how rights are passed on, not well-formed transactions.

questions.prompt: Which model is also called the "Chinese Wall"?
questions.explanation: Brewer-Nash prevents access to competing companies' data after viewing a client's data.

whyNot.0: Clark-Wilson concerns well-formed transactions.
whyNot.2: Biba concerns integrity.

questions.prompt: Which properties are required of a reference monitor?
choices: Hosted in the cloud so that it is always available
Installed on each workstation and able to be disabled by the administrator
Always invoked, tamperproof and small enough to be verified
Fast, free, open source and easy to update
questions.explanation: It checks every access, cannot be modified and must be possible to analyze completely.

whyNot.0: Its location is not a property of the concept.
whyNot.1: It precisely must not be possible to bypass it.

questions.prompt: Which component measures the boot process and protects the disk encryption keys inside the machine?
questions.explanation: The TPM stores keys and records the boot measurements to detect a modification.

whyNot.0: The firewall filters network traffic.
whyNot.2: DNS resolves names.

questions.prompt: What is a virtual machine escape (VM escape)?
choices: The live migration of a VM to another physical host
Exploiting a hypervisor flaw to break out of a VM
Deleting an unneeded VM to reduce the attack surface
Backing up a VM as a snapshot
questions.explanation: The hypervisor is part of the TCB: a flaw compromises the isolation between all the VMs.

whyNot.0: Migration is a normal operation.
whyNot.2: That is routine administration.

questions.prompt: A laboratory wants to prevent validated experiment results from being modified based on unverified raw data. Which model fits best?
choices: None, it is an availability problem
questions.explanation: This is about integrity: a less reliable source is not allowed to contaminate more reliable data.

whyNot.1: There is no conflict of interest.
whyNot.2: It is an integrity problem.

questions.prompt: Which phrase sums up Zero Trust?
choices: Trust everything inside the internal network
questions.explanation: No implicit trust: every access is explicitly verified.

whyNot.0: Zero Trust strengthens authentication; it does not remove it.
whyNot.2: That is the perimeter model that Zero Trust challenges.
whyNot.3: Zero Trust controls access; it does not cut everything off.

questions.prompt: In the NIST Zero Trust architecture, which component decides whether to grant access?
questions.explanation: The PDP (policy engine and policy administrator) decides; the PEP enforces the decision in front of the resource.

whyNot.0: The switch does not evaluate the Zero Trust policy.
whyNot.1: The PEP enforces the decision; it does not make it.
whyNot.2: DNS does not make access decisions.

questions.prompt: In a SaaS service, who remains responsible for managing accounts and access rights?
questions.explanation: In every cloud model, data and access remain the customer's responsibility.

whyNot.0: The provider manages the application, not who accesses it on the customer's side.
whyNot.2: Responsibility never disappears.
whyNot.3: The browser plays no role in access management.

questions.prompt: Why is the perimeter security model no longer enough?
choices: Because the Internet has become too slow to go through a perimeter
Because perimeter firewalls are no longer sold
Because encrypting traffic leaving the network is prohibited
Because users and attackers are also outside the network
questions.explanation: Remote work, the cloud and credential theft make network location an unreliable criterion for trust.

whyNot.0: Unrelated.
whyNot.2: False.

questions.prompt: Which elements are among the pillars of the CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model? (several answers)
questions.explanation: The five pillars are: identity, devices, networks, applications and workloads, data.

whyNot.0: Printers are devices, but they do not form a separate pillar.

questions.prompt: In an IaaS model, who applies the operating system patches on the virtual machines?
questions.explanation: In IaaS, the provider manages the hardware and virtualization; the guest system is the customer's responsibility.

whyNot.0: It does not manage the customer's systems.
whyNot.2: It manages the infrastructure below the hypervisor.
whyNot.3: Nothing is automatic without configuration by the customer.

questions.prompt: What does ZTNA offer compared with a classic remote access VPN?
choices: The user accesses the whole internal network, as if they were in the office
It replaces encryption with network address translation (NAT)
It removes authentication, replaced by the device's IP address
The user only accesses authorized applications, based on their context
questions.explanation: ZTNA grants per-application access, decided according to identity and context, instead of broad network access.

whyNot.0: That is the classic drawback of the VPN.
whyNot.2: It strengthens authentication.

questions.prompt: Which measure most directly applies the "assume breach" principle?
choices: Removing internal logging to reduce the volume of data
Microsegmenting and monitoring to limit and spot an intruder already inside
Opening internal flows to simplify administration and troubleshooting
Trusting headquarters workstations, already protected by the perimeter
questions.explanation: If the attacker is already inside, you limit what they can reach and detect them quickly.

whyNot.0: Detection would be lost.
whyNot.2: That makes lateral movement easier.

questions.prompt: A vendor promises "Zero Trust in a single box". What is the best response?
choices: Buy the box immediately to become Zero Trust compliant as quickly as possible
Point out that Zero Trust is a strategy, and assess what the product covers
Replace the SOC with this box, since it covers the whole Zero Trust strategy
Refuse every market solution and develop everything in-house to keep control
questions.explanation: No single product delivers Zero Trust; each solution is assessed against the pillars.

whyNot.0: That confuses a tool with a strategy.
whyNot.2: Human monitoring remains essential.
whyNot.3: Products help, without being enough on their own.

questions.prompt: A cloud storage bucket containing customer data is left open to the public by mistake. Who is responsible?
choices: The customer, who manages the configuration and access to its data
The cloud provider, which hosts the storage
Nobody, it is a technical failure
questions.explanation: Configuring access to the data is always the customer's job in the shared responsibility model.

whyNot.1: The provider supplies the settings; it does not decide to make the data public.
whyNot.2: The ISP plays no role here.
whyNot.3: It is a human error, not a failure.
